Remember that we can represent a system of two linear equations in two variables using matrices. We can do the same thing for a system of three linear equations in three variables, such as the following:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}3x+2y\text{ }-\text{ }2z &=7 \\ 2x\text{ }-\text{ }1y\text{ }-\text{ }4z &=2 \\ 2x+1y\text{ }-\text{ }3z &=3\end{aligned}\right.
$$

For a $3 \times 3$ system like the one above, we put the coefficients of the system into a $3 \times 3$ coefficient matrix:



$$
A= \begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}3} & {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}-2} \\ {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}-1} & {\color{blue}-4} \\ {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}-3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$



Each row has the coefficients of one of the equations in the system, and each column consists of the coefficients of one particular variable.
We also have the $3 \times 1$ column vectors



$$
\mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix}{\color{red}7} \\ {\color{red}2} \\ {\color{red}3}\end{bmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{x} = \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix},
$$



where $\mathbf{b}$ consists of each constant on the right side of the system and $\mathbf{x}$ contains the variables.
With these matrices, we can write our system as $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b},$ or



$$
\begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}3} & {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}-2} \\ {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}-1} & {\color{blue}-4} \\ {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}-3}\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}x \\ y \\ z\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}{\color{red}7} \\ {\color{red}2} \\ {\color{red}3}\end{bmatrix}.
$$



We can write any system of three equations with three variables in this form. Just to check that the above equation is true, let's multiply out the left-hand side to see if it equals the right-hand side:

$$

$$

To compute the product of an elementary matrix and another matrix, one option is to perform the matrix multiplication as usual. However, there's an easier, quicker way.

Remember that every elementary matrix is the result of applying an elementary row operation to the identity matrix. If we multiply another matrix by an elementary matrix, we're effectively applying the elementary row operation to the other matrix.

For example, suppose we are asked to find the product $EA$ where
$$
E = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{array} \right]} \quad \textrm{and} \quad A = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{red}3} & {\color{red}4} \\ {\color{blue}8} & {\color{blue}6}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

The elementary matrix $E$ comes from swapping the two rows of the identity matrix ($R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2$). So, to compute the product $EA,$ all we have to do is swap the two rows of $A\mathbin{:}$
$$
EA = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{blue}8} & {\color{blue}6} \\ {\color{red}3} & {\color{red}4}\end{array} \right]}
$$

This may seem almost too easy. But it's true! And we can verify it by computing the product the long way, using matrix multiplication. Indeed, we get the same result:

$$
\begin{aligned}EA & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 4 \\ 8 & 6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 6 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we say that $E \cdot A$ is equivalent to applying to $A$ the elementary row operation $R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2.$

**Watch out!** It's important to multiply $A$ from the *left*. If we multiply $A$ by an elementary matrix from the *right*, we will perform a *column* operation on $A$ (not a row operation). In this case, multiplying $A$ by $E$ from the right will have the effect of switching the *columns* of $A,$ not the rows.

$$
\begin{aligned}AE & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 4 \\ 8 & 6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 3 \\ 6 & 8\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$
